name: MAS Director's Dilemma — Redesigning a Swiss Flagship Under a Margin Floor
description: A four-round, advanced continuing-education leadership simulation set at Limmat School of Management, the continuing-education arm of a Swiss university of applied sciences in Zürich. You direct its flagship MAS Business Administration — a 12-module, part-time qualification for working professionals. Over three years intake has fallen from 96 to 71 students, the programme now contributes only ~12% margin against an 18% floor set by the university finance office, completion sits at 81% (benchmark 88%), and a competitor has just launched a modular, employer-co-designed certificate stack at 30% lower total cost. The dean's office gives you one design cycle to bring the September intake back to viability — or the MAS is suspended or merged into a cheaper stackable format. Every currency figure is in Swiss francs (CHF). Round 1 — diagnose the programme: separate the real demand signal (employers want applied relevance; learners want flexibility) from noise, apply minimum-viable-cohort logic (below ~60 students the partly-fixed cost base of faculty, rooms and platform isn't covered), and frame the central tension. Round 2 — set the curriculum mix: rebalance the 12 modules toward applied, sector-relevant content without gutting the generalist core that makes it a Master's, and build stackability deliberately so a CAS entry funnels into the full MAS rather than cannibalising the high-margin later modules. Round 3 — price and sequence together: model the elasticity (a 10% tuition rise costs ~8–10 enrolments) against the margin floor and the competitor's cheaper stack, remembering a price cut only works if cost came out of the base; and sequence the modules to lift completion above 88% and smooth cash flow rather than front-loading the hardest module. Round 4 — defend the redesign to the dean's office: lead with the system (enrolment, margin, completion and two-sided demand fit as one coherent design), answer the stackable competitor by differentiating, and commit to the leading indicators — applications, early deposits, employer-sponsorship commitments — that predict the intake before September. The math rewards a deliberate curriculum rebalance, funnel-in stackability, disciplined pricing matched to a leaner cost base, and completion-smart sequencing — and punishes the five classic errors: a price-only margin fix that drops below the viable cohort, volume-only discounting that widens the deficit, identity loss from gutting the core, one-sided design that ignores either the paying learner or the sponsoring employer, and sequencing neglect that erodes completion. Sticky run-defining penalty flags gate the top verdict so a single strong round cannot wash out a fatal error, while a balanced, in-budget redesign can genuinely restore the flagship. Final KPIs track projected September enrolment, contribution margin (%), completion rate (%), and a two-sided demand-fit index.

Your Design Decisions This Round

Current variable cost ≈ CHF 15,500/student. Converting modules to applied delivery and protecting margin usually means taking cost out; gutting the core or over-building adds cost.
Current CHF 28,000. Elasticity: each 10% rise costs ~8–10 enrolments. Competitor stack is ~30% cheaper. A cut only helps if cost came out in Round 2.
The dean’s office (your facilitator)
The MAS has run below its 18% margin floor for two consecutive intakes. You have one design cycle. Raise tuition to fix the ratio and you risk falling below the 60-student viable cohort; cut it without cutting cost and you widen the deficit; gut the generalist core to please employers and the credential stops being a Master’s. Redesign the mix, the price and the sequence as one system — and bring the September intake back to viability without losing what makes it the MAS.
